mcqs.q: Dental plaque is best described as:
opts: A structured, resilient biofilm that adheres tenaciously and is not removed by rinsing
A soft deposit easily washed off with a water spray
A salivary film containing no bacteria
mcqs.explain: Plaque is a structured biofilm; materia alba washes off; calculus is mineralized plaque.

mcqs.q: Materia alba differs from plaque in that it:
opts: Is loosely adherent and can be flushed off with a water spray
mcqs.explain: Materia alba is a soft, loosely adherent mixture of bacteria, debris and cells, removable by water spray.

mcqs.q: Calculus is essentially:
opts: Mineralized plaque covered by a living plaque layer
mcqs.explain: Calculus is calcified plaque; its rough surface is always covered by a layer of viable plaque.

mcqs.q: Approximately what proportion of the SOLID component of plaque is bacteria?
mcqs.explain: Bacteria make up ~70–80% of plaque solids (plaque is ~80% water overall); 1 mg ≈ 250 million bacteria.

mcqs.q: The FIRST event in plaque formation is:
mcqs.explain: The acquired pellicle forms first, then initial adhesion, then colonization/maturation.

mcqs.q: Marginal supragingival plaque is clinically important because it:
opts: Lies at the gingival margin and is the key initiator of gingivitis
Is located deep within the periodontal pocket
Cannot be stained by disclosing agents
mcqs.explain: Supragingival plaque is coronal (tooth) or marginal (at the gingival margin); marginal plaque drives gingival inflammation.

mcqs.q: Subgingival plaque, being within the sulcus/pocket, is:
opts: Usually thin and not detectable by direct observation — found by running a probe around the margin
Thick and easily seen without a probe
mcqs.explain: Subgingival plaque is thin and hidden; its presence is detected by probing the margin.

mcqs.q: Tooth-associated (attached) subgingival plaque is dominated by:
opts: Gram-positive cocci, rods and filamentous bacteria
mcqs.explain: Attached (tooth-associated) plaque resembles supragingival plaque — Gram-positive cocci/rods/filaments; it is linked to calculus and root caries/resorption.

mcqs.q: Epithelium-associated (unattached) subgingival plaque characteristically:
opts: Lacks a matrix and is rich in Gram-negative rods, flagellates and spirochetes
Is firmly attached, with an abundant interbacterial matrix
Contains only Gram-positive cocci and no other forms
Is essentially the same material as calculus
mcqs.explain: Loosely adherent, matrix-poor plaque in direct contact with the epithelium; predominantly Gram-negative, flagellated and spirochetal.

mcqs.q: The main 'bridging' organism linking early and late colonizers is:
mcqs.explain: F. nucleatum coaggregates with both early (Strep/Actinomyces) and late colonizers, bridging the two.

mcqs.q: Primary (early) colonizers of the tooth surface are mainly:
mcqs.explain: Early colonizers are predominantly Gram-positive Streptococcus and Actinomyces.

mcqs.q: S. sanguis can antagonize A. actinomycetemcomitans by producing:
mcqs.explain: S. sanguis produces H₂O₂, which can kill A. actinomycetemcomitans — a beneficial antagonistic interaction.

mcqs.q: Socransky's 'red complex' (most associated with periodontitis) comprises:
opts: P. gingivalis, T. forsythia and T. denticola
S. sanguinis, S. mitis and A. oris
F. nucleatum, P. intermedia and P. micra
mcqs.explain: The red complex = P. gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola — the most pathogenic cluster.

mcqs.q: In the older 'localized aggressive periodontitis', which organism may comprise up to 90% of the cultivable microbiota?
mcqs.explain: A. actinomycetemcomitans predominates in localized aggressive periodontitis (up to ~90%).

mcqs.q: Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG) is associated with high proportions of:
mcqs.explain: NUG shows abundant spirochetes and F. nucleatum (fusospirochetal complex).

mcqs.q: The NONSPECIFIC plaque hypothesis holds that periodontal disease results from:
opts: The noxious products of the entire plaque flora (total quantity)
A keystone pathogen at low abundance
mcqs.explain: Nonspecific hypothesis = disease from the whole plaque mass; specific hypothesis = particular pathogens; ecological/keystone are later refinements.

mcqs.q: The keystone-pathogen hypothesis proposes that:
opts: P. gingivalis, even in low numbers, remodels a benign microbiota into a dysbiotic one
Only the total amount of plaque matters
Bacteria play no role in periodontitis
mcqs.explain: P. gingivalis acts as a low-abundance keystone pathogen, driving dysbiosis and disease.

mcqs.q: Which best defines dysbiosis in the periodontal context?
opts: A shift of the resident microbiota from a balanced/benign community to a disease-associated one
mcqs.explain: Dysbiosis is an imbalance of the microbial community favoring pathogens, driven by environmental change/keystone pathogens.

mcqs.q: The acquired pellicle coats a cleaned tooth surface within:
mcqs.explain: It is a thin film of salivary glycoproteins, proteins and lipids.

mcqs.q: The acquired pellicle promotes bacterial adhesion because it:
opts: Changes the surface charge and energy, providing receptors for bacterial adhesion
Supplies nutrients directly to the bacteria
Lowers the pH at the tooth surface
mcqs.explain: Pellicle formation is therefore the first of the three stages of plaque formation.

mcqs.q: Which organisms are SECONDARY colonizers of the biofilm?
opts: P. intermedia, F. nucleatum, Capnocytophaga and Prevotella
S. sanguinis, S. mitis and A. oris
P. gingivalis, T. forsythia and T. denticola
mcqs.explain: They attach to the primary colonizers by coaggregation; the red complex dominates established periodontitis.

mcqs.q: The colour of supragingival plaque varies from:
mcqs.explain: Small amounts are revealed with disclosing agents.

mcqs.q: The INORGANIC component of plaque consists chiefly of:
opts: Calcium and phosphorus, with traces of sodium, potassium and fluoride
mcqs.explain: As the mineral content rises, plaque calcifies into calculus; fluoride can be incorporated and used in caries prevention.

mcqs.q: Besides polysaccharides and proteins, the plaque matrix contains glycoproteins, lipid material and DNA. Albumin in the matrix originates from:
mcqs.explain: Bacteria make up about 70–80% of the solid material; the rest is extracellular matrix.

mcqs.q: The microbiota of periodontal HEALTH is dominated by:
mcqs.explain: It is a stable, low-diversity community in symbiosis with the host.

mcqs.q: In gingivitis the microbiota shifts towards:
opts: Greater diversity with more Gram-negative and anaerobic species
Lower diversity with more Gram-positive species
A pure culture of A. actinomycetemcomitans
mcqs.explain: Capnocytophaga, Fusobacterium, Prevotella, Campylobacter, V. parvula, Haemophilus and E. corrodens are among the Gram-negatives involved.

mcqs.q: Which viruses are implicated in periodontitis?
opts: EBV-1 and HCMV of the herpesvirus group
mcqs.explain: They are implicated alongside the red complex and organisms such as P. intermedia and C. rectus.

mcqs.q: In localised aggressive periodontitis, A. actinomycetemcomitans may comprise as much as:
mcqs.explain: It typically affects the first molars and incisors in adolescents.

mcqs.q: Generalised aggressive periodontitis is dominated more by:
opts: P. gingivalis, P. intermedia, T. forsythia and Treponema — less by A. a.
A. actinomycetemcomitans acting entirely on its own
mcqs.explain: High proportions of E. nodatum, Campylobacter gracilis, Campylobacter showae and P. nigrescens are also found.

mcqs.q: The CONSTANT flora of necrotizing periodontal disease (NUG/NUP) consists of:
opts: P. gingivalis and T. forsythia only
mcqs.explain: There is also a variable flora, and overall a high proportion of anaerobic Gram-negative rods, motile organisms and spirochetes.

mcqs.q: The SPECIFIC plaque hypothesis differs from the nonspecific hypothesis in that it:
opts: Qualitative — only certain specific pathogens actually cause disease
The more plaque there is, the more disease results
Disease is attributable to environmental change alone
Bacteria play no role at all in periodontal disease
mcqs.explain: It explains why some heavily-colonized sites stay healthy while others with specific pathogens break down.

mcqs.q: The ECOLOGICAL plaque hypothesis proposes that disease results from:
opts: An imbalance in the resident microbiota driven by a change in local environmental conditions
The sheer quantity of plaque alone
A single specific pathogen acting in isolation
Viral infection of the gingival tissues
mcqs.explain: Inflammation, gingival crevicular fluid and a raised pH favour the overgrowth of Gram-negative anaerobes — linking quantity and specificity.

mcqs.q: 'Polymicrobial synergy and dysbiosis' (PSD) proposes that disease arises from:
opts: The community acting as a pathogen, rather than one species alone
A single keystone species acting alone
The total mass of plaque only
Host factors with no microbial contribution
mcqs.explain: The keystone-pathogen hypothesis complements it: P. gingivalis can remodel a benign microbiota into a dysbiotic one even at low numbers.

mcqs.q: The mainstay of biofilm management is:
opts: Mechanical biofilm disruption — oral hygiene, scaling and root planing
mcqs.explain: Probiotics, prebiotics and antibiotics or antiseptics in selected cases are adjuncts; the goal is to shift the community back toward a symbiotic state.

saqs.q: Differentiate dental plaque, materia alba and calculus.
saqs.a: PLAQUE — a structured, resilient biofilm (~70–80% bacteria in a matrix) adhering tenaciously, not removed by rinsing. MATERIA ALBA — soft, loosely adherent bacteria, food debris and cells, flushed off with a water spray. CALCULUS — mineralized plaque, always covered by living plaque, acting as a plaque-retentive surface.

a soft, loosely adherent accumulation of bacteria, food debris and cells — flushed off with a water spray
mineralized (calcified) plaque, always covered by a layer of living plaque, acting as a plaque-retentive surface

saqs.q: Describe the three stages of plaque formation.
saqs.a: 1 Acquired pellicle — a thin salivary glycoprotein film within minutes. 2 Initial adhesion and attachment — bacteria bind to the pellicle. 3 Colonization and maturation — growth, coaggregation and a mature biofilm.

steps: ACQUIRED PELLICLE — a thin salivary glycoprotein film coats the tooth within minutes
INITIAL ADHESION AND ATTACHMENT — bacteria bind to the pellicle
COLONIZATION AND MATURATION — bacterial growth, coaggregation and development of a mature biofilm

saqs.q: Compare tooth-associated and epithelium-associated subgingival plaque.
saqs.a: TOOTH-ASSOCIATED (attached) — resembles supragingival plaque; Gram-positive cocci, rods and filaments, with a matrix; linked to calculus, root caries and root resorption. EPITHELIUM-ASSOCIATED (unattached) — loosely adherent, no interbacterial matrix, in direct contact with the sulcular/junctional epithelium; Gram-negative rods and cocci, flagellated bacteria and spirochetes.

saqs.q: Explain bacterial colonization of the biofilm, naming primary colonizers, the bridging organism and late colonizers.
saqs.a: PRIMARY (early) — Gram-positive Streptococcus and Actinomyces (S. sanguinis, S. mitis, A. naeslundii). BRIDGING — Fusobacterium nucleatum, coaggregating with both early and late colonizers. SECONDARY (late) — Gram-negative anaerobes: P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola, P. intermedia, Capnocytophaga.

saqs.q: Outline the evolution of plaque-disease hypotheses.
saqs.a: NONSPECIFIC — the noxious products of the whole flora (total quantity). SPECIFIC — only specific pathogens (qualitative composition). ECOLOGICAL — an environmental change selects pathogens. KEYSTONE-PATHOGEN — a low-abundance keystone (P. gingivalis) remodels a benign microbiota into a dysbiotic one.

saqs.q: Describe the microbiota associated with periodontal health, gingivitis and periodontitis.
saqs.a: HEALTH — Gram-positive facultative Streptococcus and Actinomyces; stable, low-diversity, in symbiosis. GINGIVITIS — greater diversity, more Gram-negative and anaerobic species. PERIODONTITIS — the RED COMPLEX (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) with P. intermedia, P. nigrescens, C. rectus and E. corrodens; herpesviruses EBV-1 and HCMV also implicated.
